blocks.text: 1. The Update Gate

blocks.alt: The previous hidden state feeds the update gate to interpolate old and new

blocks.text: GRU Architecture, the previous topic, introduced two gates replacing LSTM's own three. The Update Gate gives a complete, dedicated look at GRU's first of two gates, explored in full depth throughout this topic.
It decides how much of the previous hidden state to genuinely keep versus replace, a genuinely important, foundational mechanism covered throughout the rest of this topic.
2. Recapping The Preview

This connects back to two gates instead of three, already covered in GRU Architecture. The update gate was genuinely introduced there as the first of GRU's two gates, briefly described in that earlier topic.
This topic genuinely gives it the complete, dedicated treatment already promised, exploring every mathematical and practical detail already hinted at throughout GRU Architecture.
3. A Combined Role, Explained

blocks.alt: The forget role and input role are combined in one gate

blocks.text: This connects back to the forget gate and input gate, both already covered in their own LSTM topics. The update gate genuinely combines the roles those two separate LSTM gates played.
It decides both how much old information to keep and how much new information to add, together, exactly the two-in-one simplification already previewed generally in GRU Architecture.

blocks.text: 4. The Core Operation

The update gate's genuinely core operation connects back to the Sigmoid gating mechanism, already covered in LSTM Architecture. Compute a Sigmoid value from the current input and previous hidden state, the exact same familiar pattern.

This directly reuses the exact same gating computation already covered throughout every LSTM gate, keeping GRU's own overall design genuinely consistent with the broader gating philosophy already covered in this module.
5. The Interpolation Formula

blocks.alt: The old hidden state and new candidate interpolate into the new hidden state

blocks.text: This connects back to the candidate values, already covered in The Input Gate. The new hidden state genuinely blends the old hidden state and new candidate values using the update gate's own value.
This is a genuinely smooth interpolation between keeping the past and adopting the new, a genuinely direct, elegant formula that gives GRU its own distinctive update mechanism.
6. One Gate, Two Decisions

blocks.alt: The update gate decides how much old to keep and how much new to add

blocks.text: A genuinely elegant mathematical insight connects back to the update gate's own single Sigmoid value, already covered in this topic. A genuinely high update gate value means keep more old information.
A genuinely low value means adopt more new information instead, a genuinely elegant, single-parameter way of controlling both decisions already covered as LSTM's own separate forget and input gates.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: This elegant, single-parameter tradeoff, already covered in this topic, is exactly why the update gate needs no genuinely separate normalization step: keeping more old information automatically means adopting proportionally less new information.

blocks.text: 7. Versus Forget And Input Together

blocks.alt: LSTM uses forget and input gates while GRU uses one update gate

blocks.text: This connects back to gradient summation, already covered in Backpropagation Through Time. LSTM genuinely needed two genuinely separate gates, forget and input, computed independently, already covered throughout that module.
GRU's own single update gate, already covered in this topic, genuinely ties these two decisions together instead, a genuinely direct structural simplification already previewed in GRU Architecture.

blocks.text: 8. A Direct Contributor To Fewer Parameters

blocks.alt: The update gate contributes to fewer parameters than LSTM

blocks.text: This connects back to the benefit of fewer parameters, already covered in GRU Architecture. Combining two decisions into one gate genuinely means one fewer full set of gate weights to learn.
This is a genuinely direct, concrete contributor to the parameter reduction already covered there, showing precisely where GRU's own efficiency advantage over LSTM actually comes from.
9. Recognizing Why The Update Gate Is Genuinely Essential

blocks.alt: Needing to balance old and new information points toward the update gate

blocks.text: This connects back to needing to balance old and new information smoothly, already covered throughout this topic. The update gate, already covered in this topic, directly provides that genuinely smooth balancing mechanism.
This connects back to GRU's own overall simplification goal, already covered in GRU Architecture. The update gate, already covered, is genuinely a core piece of achieving that simplification.
10. Worked Example
The example below directly demonstrates the update gate's own interpolation formula, blending old and new hidden state values, illustrating the concepts already covered throughout this topic.

code.content:
import numpy as np

def sigmoid(x):
    return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-x))

old_hidden_state = np.array([2.0, -1.0, 0.5, 3.0])
candidate_values = np.array([0.2, 1.5, -0.8, 0.1])  # already covered as new candidate values in this topic

# already covered as the core operation in this topic
update_gate_high = sigmoid(np.array([3.0, 3.0, 3.0, 3.0]))  # close to 1, favors keeping old
update_gate_low = sigmoid(np.array([-3.0, -3.0, -3.0, -3.0]))  # close to 0, favors adopting new

# already covered as the interpolation formula in this topic
new_hidden_high = update_gate_high * old_hidden_state + (1 - update_gate_high) * candidate_values
new_hidden_low = update_gate_low * old_hidden_state + (1 - update_gate_low) * candidate_values

print("Old hidden state:", old_hidden_state)
print("Candidate values:", candidate_values)
print(f"\nWith a high update gate (favors keeping old): {np.round(new_hidden_high, 3)}")
print(f"With a low update gate (favors adopting new): {np.round(new_hidden_low, 3)}")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Running this example shows a high update gate value keeping the result genuinely close to the old hidden state, while a low value pulls it genuinely close to the new candidate values, exactly the interpolation already covered in this topic.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: The update gate decides how much of the previous hidden state to keep versus replace.
It combines the roles LSTM's separate forget gate and input gate played.
It computes a Sigmoid value from the current input and previous hidden state, like LSTM's gates.
The new hidden state smoothly interpolates between the old hidden state and new candidate values.
A high update gate value means keep more old information; a low value means adopt more new information.
This ties keep-versus-add into one decision, unlike LSTM's two independent gates.
Combining two decisions into one gate is a direct contributor to GRU's fewer parameters.
It provides GRU's smooth balancing mechanism between old and new information.
